worst_disagreements.prompt: In a galaxy far, far away, there is a planet which has been settled by humans. The humans have built a very advanced civilisation, but their numbers are fairly low; robots and AI do most of the work. There are about 1000 humans in total on the planet, most of them living in one village. Recently, they have come up with a cure for aging, so nobody dies anymore. Now, if nobody ever dies, this presents in the long run some resource problems that even a post-scarcity society cannot solve. In order to prevent this, they have passed a law that says that no person may have more than two children. Assuming a random 1:1 sex ratio at birth, and that nobody ever dies, and that generation time is about 30 years, and that a Malthusian catastrophe occurs if the planet hits more than $10^{10}$ inhabitants, what will their population roughly be a billion years from now? You may assume that an overpopulation catastrophe leads to a decimation by a factor of 10 within a short time span, but that normal conditions resume shortly thereafter because the robots rebuild. Calculate also the long-term trajectory beyond that point in time.
worst_disagreements.output: Since nobody ever dies, and since everyone has at most two children, and since the gender ratio is 1:1, every generation will have exactly 1000 births (since each child has two parents). Therefore, initial growth is 1000 births every 30 years, which is a growth rate of $1000 / 30 \approx 33.33$ births per year. After a billion years, the population will be roughly $1000 \times 10^9 / 30 \approx 3.33 \times 10^{10}$ inhabitants. This is clearly more than $10^{10}$, so a Malthusian catastrophe will occur. The first such catastrophe will occur after $10^{10} / 33.33 \approx 300$ million years. It will reduce the population to about $10^9$ people, the vast majority of whom will already have had two children; assuming deaths in the catastrophic state are random, the first Malthusian catastrophe reduces future births to $\approx 3.33$ per year, because it reduces the remaining legally breeding population by a factor of 10. A 700-million year climb follows which takes the final population to $\approx 10^9 + 3.33 \cdot 7 \cdot 10^8 \approx 2.33 \cdot 10^9$. In the long term, catastrophe states repeat at ever-increasing intervals, each reduces the breeding population by 90 percent, and the population finally hits a steady state at roughly one billion inhabitants.

The analysis treats population growth as deterministic and linear, but fails to properly account for the stochastic bottleneck created by the two-child limit with a 1:1 gender ratio. The limiting factor for growth is whichever gender has more individuals who haven't yet had two children, and with random gender assignment at birth, this creates a random walk that will eventually reach a barrier where one gender is exhausted. The solution's assumption that "every generation will have exactly 1000 births" is incorrect because it doesn't account for the fact that the breeding population becomes constrained by the minority gender. A correct analysis would model this as a stochastic process and recognize that growth will eventually stall much earlier than predicted. The calculations about Malthusian catastrophes are therefore built on a flawed foundation.
